label: rejudged

results.requestText: What should I wear to work tomorrow?

looks.title: Check Blazer, Finally Worn
looks.idea: A rust-and-brown check blazer over stripes, sharpened with a belted waist.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the Breton top into the navy cigarette trousers and put the wide black belt at your natural waist. Wear the oversized blazer open with the sleeves pushed up just to the wrist bone. The slim cropped trouser keeps the proportions balanced under the boyfriend-fit jacket. Add the gold hoops and carry the black tote. Wear the camel coat over the top for the walk and the Tube.
looks.why: This is the one piece you haven't yet found a use for, and it makes a strong pitch-ready jacket. The rust and cream in the check warm up the navy stripe, and print-on-print is your signature. The slim trouser and belt mark your waist so the oversized blazer doesn't swamp you, which is the lesson from the tulle and cable-knit day. Black Chelsea boots are fine in drizzle, and your arms stay covered. It's polished without the default black blazer.

looks.title: Pink Tweed and Florals
looks.idea: Colour-on-colour joy with one sharp, cropped jacket.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the cobalt merino into the high-rise floral wide-leg trousers so the waist is clear. Put the cropped pink tweed jacket over it, worn open, and let the hem sit right at your waistline. Pull the trousers up so the hems skim the top of the red Mary Janes. Add the gold hoops, a few bangles over the jumper cuff, and the red mini bag. The belted trench goes over the top for drizzle.
looks.why: This repeats your navy floral and cobalt combination, which felt joyful, and adds the tweed jacket you've worn only once. The pink picks up the pink in the trousers. The cropped jacket and high rise suit your waist and short-legged proportions. The tweed gives the outfit a sharp, polished element for the office. Cobalt and red are in your best colours, and your arms are fully covered.

looks.title: Baroque Wrap, Dressed Down for Drizzle
looks.idea: Your most-complimented dress, made sharp and weatherproof for the office.
looks.howToWear: Wear the wrap dress with the black opaque tights and the flat knee-high boots, with the hem falling at or just over the boot tops so the leg line stays unbroken. Wear the burgundy beret slightly back off the face. Add the gold hoops and stacked bangles. Wear the belted trench over the dress, cinched tight, and carry the black tote.
looks.why: The wrap dress is already your most flattering piece, with a defined waist, long sleeves and a polished formality of 4/5, so it handles a client pitch without any extra effort. Dark tights and boots in the same colour make your legs look longer. The beret picks up the burgundy in the print and keeps your hair dry in the drizzle. The black stays at the feet and the coat, away from your face. Leather boots and a water-resistant trench suit a wet commute.

output.note: I left the black tailored blazer in the wardrobe on purpose, since each look here has a more interesting sharp element. Avoid the tan suede boots tomorrow because of the drizzle.

failures.detail: Taking m45 out of the wardrobe is the right instinct. But pairing it with the Breton m06, navy cigarettes m27 and all-black accessories gives a French-preppy uniform with no warm bright and no romance. It reads closer to 'smart heritage' than to Dries or Susie Bubble.

The hip-length boyfriend blazer cuts her at the hip. The ankle-cropped m27 trousers then shorten legs that are already short relative to her torso. Worn open over a wide black belt, the waist only shows as a narrow vertical strip.

The camel wool coat m50 is the only outerwear here that isn't water-resistant, and it's chosen on a drizzle day. Pale camel also marks with rain spots. The trench m51 would have been the better commute layer.

'Print-on-print is your signature' is overstated for a narrow stripe under a check. It doesn't explain the brown-check-with-black-leather choice. 'Sleeves pushed up just to the wrist bone' is not a real styling move.

looks.comment: A good rescue of the never-worn m45, and the cream thread linking check and stripe is sound. But the result is tasteful rather than joyful: it uses her most expressive orphan piece in her least expressive way.

failures.detail: The red mini bag m74 is too small for a full office day. Full-length crepe wide-legs m20 with flats will wick drizzle at the hem on the walk to the Tube. Keeping the black tote m71 as a carry-all, or rolling the hems for the commute, would help.
Bangles stacked over a merino cuff sit awkwardly under a jacket sleeve. Gold hoops alone would be cleaner. The boucle m42 is soft rather than sharp, so the 'one sharp element' is a bit of a stretch.

looks.comment: This is the look that sounds most like Maya. It builds on her proven m20 + m10 + m62 combination and adds the barely-worn pink tweed m42, cropped exactly at her waist to lengthen the leg line. Pink, cobalt and red is a genuinely joyful clash with logic, because the pink in the floral sanctions it.

failures.detail: This is essentially a weatherised repeat of her best-known hit, m30. Black tights, black boots, black trench and black tote make it read darker and more sombre than her colour-forward DNA. The red Mary Janes or the tan crossbody m70 could have kept one warm note below the waist.

looks.comment: The most weather-proof and pitch-ready look of the three. Tonal black tights into the flat knee boots m67 under a midi hem is a correct leg-lengthening move, and the burgundy beret m87 is a smart pick-up from the print. One caveat: once the trench is buttoned, the black collar sits at her face despite the claim otherwise.

judgement.missedOpportunity: Wear the check blazer m45 over the leopard silk blouse m01, tucked into the camel corduroy flares m26, with black Chelsea boots m60 hidden under the flare. Add gold hoops m80, the tan crossbody m70 and the black trench m51. The leopard-and-check tonal mix is the Dries/Gucci move m45 was bought for. The high-rise flare lengthens her legs, and the warm brown palette suits her colouring far better than navy stripe with black leather.
judgement.summary: A solid, wearable set with real range: a tailored trouser look, a colour-on-colour look and a dress. Every look respects the arms-covered and heel directives and suits a drizzly 9°C day. Look 2 is the standout and most 'her'. Look 3 is the safest and most polished, though it leans heavily on black. Look 1 deserves credit for finally wearing m45 but styles it too conservatively, with awkward proportions and a non-waterproof camel coat. Before sending, consider: swap the m50 coat for the trench, add a larger bag to Look 2, and push Look 1 toward the warmer leopard pairing.

results.requestText: Dinner with friends at a nice restaurant on Saturday night.

looks.title: Baroque Romance, Rain-Ready
looks.idea: Her proven baroque wrap dress, kept sharp with flat knee-high boots and a red bag for a pop.
looks.howToWear: Tie the wrap snugly at the natural waist. Wear black opaque tights with the flat knee-high boots so the leg line runs unbroken from hem to boot. Stack the bangles on one wrist and wear the hoops with hair back. Carry the red mini bag on its short strap. Wear the trench belted over the top on the way there, then hang it up at the restaurant so the dress shows.
looks.why: This is the spirit of her gallery-opening look, which got compliments and felt like her: wrap dress, gold hoops, a warm-toned boot. The boots are waterproof enough for drizzle and flat for the Tube and walking. The tights and boots lengthen her shorter legs, and the red bag adds a warm bright without competing with the print. The black trench goes over the dress and comes off indoors, so it can't make the dress feel corporate.

looks.title: Emerald Velvet, Pink Tweed
looks.idea: Jewel-toned velvet made romantic and sharp with a cropped pink bouclé jacket.
looks.howToWear: Wear the velvet slip with black tights and the flat knee-high boots, so the bias hem skims the boot tops. Put the cropped tweed jacket on open or lightly buttoned. It stops at the waist, so it marks her waist and keeps the slip's line long. Add the pearl drops for a romantic edge and carry the beaded clutch. Put the camel coat over everything for the walk.
looks.why: Emerald is one of her best warm brights and works beautifully with her colouring. The velvet slip had only one outing. The pink and cream tweed is also barely worn and gives the sharp, polished element without a black blazer, which flattened her red dress. Cropped over a slip dress gives a defined waist, and the camel coat suits the colours and the 9°C weather.

looks.title: Check Blazer, Gold Satin
looks.idea: Tonal autumn colours and a mix of prints, with an oversized check blazer finally put to work.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the gold satin camisole into the navy cigarette trousers and cinch it with the wide black belt at the waist. Wear the oversized check blazer open over it with the sleeves pushed up to the forearm, so you see the belt and the drape of the satin. Wear the black Chelsea boots, hoops and bangles, and carry the tan crossbody. Put the camel coat over the top.
looks.why: The check blazer has never been worn because everything she tried it with got swamped. A slim, ankle-skimming trouser and a close-fitting camisole balance its volume, which avoids the top-and-bottom bulk that spoiled the tulle and jumper outfit. Rust, gold, navy and tan are warm and flatter her colouring. Gold satin brings in some romance and shine for the evening. The belt keeps her waist visible under a boyfriend cut, and the Chelsea boots handle drizzle.

output.note: I kept suede and calf-hair shoes out of tonight's looks because of the drizzle. The black Chelsea boots or flat knee-high boots are your best wet-weather options. Your wardrobe has no dressy flat that's both waterproof and colourful. If it stays dry on the night, the tan suede block-heel boots would work with the baroque dress or the check blazer look.

failures.detail: This is essentially her gallery-opening outfit (m30 + m80) with the boot swapped for wet weather. It is reliable, but it adds nothing new for a Saturday dinner.
The red m74 sits next to the burgundy in m30 rather than clearly against it, so the 'pop' is muted. A small styling note, such as keeping the bag away from the print, would help.

looks.comment: This is a sound, rain-sensible version of a proven look. The black tights and m67 boots make a continuous leg line, and the black trench (m51) comes off indoors, so it avoids the black-blazer problem. It is competent but predictable, and it is the look she would have put together herself.

failures.detail: The note says the boxy cropped m42 'marks her waist'. In reality a boxy jacket ending at the waist puts a line there but squares off her hourglass. It needs the instruction to button it at the waist, otherwise the bias slip (m38) gets no waist definition.
Velvet (m38) and bouclé (m42) are both precious in drizzle. The camel coat (m50) covers them, but it is not water-resistant like m51.

looks.comment: Pink bouclé over emerald velvet is a genuinely joyful, Gucci-toned-down colour pairing, and it puts two under-worn pieces to work. It is the strongest idea in the set. It has no print, but it is colour-forward enough to feel like her, and the pearls and beaded clutch keep it romantic.

failures.detail: Ankle-cropped m27 cigarette trousers meeting black Chelsea boots (m60) break the leg at the ankle. Under a hip-length oversized blazer (m45), that shortens legs she already wants lengthened. A high-rise wide leg would fix it.
The idea is billed as 'a mix of prints', but the only print is the check. Navy, gold, black and tan leather is not print-mixing.
The black belt (m85) and black boots (m60) sit against a tan bag (m70) and a brown/rust check. The leathers fight each other with no reason for it.
Solid navy, a single check and a camel coat read as generic autumn smart-casual rather than her eclectic, print-led DNA.

looks.comment: It is right to finally use m45, and balancing its volume with a slim bottom is sound in principle. But the cropped trouser and boot combination works against her proportions, and the look under-delivers on the print-mixing it promises. This needs a rework before it goes to the client.

judgement.missedOpportunity: A true print-mix built around the unworn check blazer: m45 over m03 gold cami tucked into m20 navy floral high-rise wide-leg trousers, with m60 Chelsea boots hidden under the wide hem for leg length in the drizzle. Add m80 hoops, m82 bangles, m74 red bag and m51 trench. Check plus floral, joined by the warm gold, is exactly her Dries/Susie Bubble territory.
judgement.summary: This is a solid set with good weather sense and an honest note about her missing waterproof dressy flat. Look 2 is the standout: emerald and pink is joyful and makes use of neglected pieces. Look 1 is a safe replay of a known win. Look 3 has the right instinct, rescuing m45, but the wrong execution: cropped trousers with ankle boots shorten her legs, the leathers clash, and it claims a print-mix it doesn't deliver. Rework Look 3 around m20 and the set becomes genuinely her.

results.requestText: Surprise me — put together something I wouldn't normally think of.

looks.title: Check Blazer, Finally
looks.idea: The never-worn check blazer over navy florals and cobalt: a print-mixed, colour-on-colour take on smart-casual.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the cobalt merino into the high-rise floral trousers and cinch the wide black belt over the jumper, so the waist shows under the oversized blazer. Wear the blazer open with the sleeves pushed up slightly to the forearm. Knot the rust silk scarf loosely at the neck, or tie it to the bag strap, to pick up the rust in the check. Chelsea boots under the full-length hems keep her dry. Camel coat on top for the walk.
looks.why: The navy floral and cobalt combination has already worked for her. The rust and brown check is the unexpected layer, and cobalt against rust is a flattering warm contrast. The belt keeps the oversized blazer from hiding her waist. It reads polished enough for a pitch, but it is print-mixed rather than corporate, and it finally gives the check blazer a job.

looks.title: Velvet by Day
looks.idea: An emerald velvet slip dress worn as a layered daytime piece: romantic, with a sharp cropped jacket.
looks.howToWear: Wear the ivory silk shirt under the slip dress with the collar out and the sleeves showing, buttoned at the cuff. Put the cropped pink tweed jacket on top, where its hem hits her natural waist. Add black opaque tights and the flat knee-high boots. Wear pearl drops and carry the red mini bag. Trench belted over everything in the drizzle.
looks.why: Layering the shirt under the slip gives full arm coverage and turns an evening dress into something for the office or an opening. Emerald and pink are warm, joyful colours near her face. The cropped jacket and bias-cut dress mark her waist and avoid the corporate black-blazer trap. The red bag adds one sharp, playful note.

looks.title: Mustard, Leopard, Burgundy
looks.idea: A warm-toned eclectic mix in which the leopard blouse sits against a pleated mustard skirt and a belted burgundy cardigan.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the leopard blouse into the high-waisted mustard skirt. Wear the burgundy longline cardigan open and belt it with the wide black belt at the waist for a defined middle and a long vertical line. Add black opaque tights and Chelsea boots, then hoops, the beret tilted back off the face, and the tan crossbody. Navy puffer on top for the cold and rain.
looks.why: This is her go-to leopard blouse in a new colour story. Mustard, burgundy and tan are all warm shades that flatter her colouring. The belted cardigan stops the pleats and longline layers from swamping her, which was the problem with the tulle and cable-knit outfit. The beret adds a romantic touch, and the puffer stays practical without being the focus.

output.note: I avoided the suede boots and calf-hair loafers because of the drizzle, and left out the mint blouse and powder blue skirt because they drain her colouring. The wardrobe has no real gaps for this brief.

failures.detail: Full-length crepe wide-legs (m20) over flat Chelsea boots (m60) will drag and wick drizzle at the hem on her shorter legs; advise a quick hem check or a slight cuff.

Minor: the scarf (m84) knotted at the neck adds a third print on top of the check and floral, and the oversized blazer (m45) under the straight camel coat (m50) will bunch at the shoulder. Tie the scarf to the bag strap instead.

looks.comment: This is the right instinct: it finally activates the never-worn check blazer (m45) on top of a combination she already knows works (m20 with m10). Rust check against cobalt and navy floral is a genuinely Dries-like mix, and the large check against the medium floral gives a proper scale contrast. The scarf-on-bag option is the better of the two.

failures.detail: A relaxed silk shirt (m13) under a bias-cut velvet slip (m38) can ruck at the waist and spoil the line. Tell her to tuck it smoothly or knot it high, and to check the sleeve bulk under the boxy boucle (m42).

It claims emerald and pink sit near her face, but the ivory collar and pink jacket do. It also misses the real teaching points: complementary emerald and pink, the texture contrast of velvet, boucle and silk, and how the knee boots plus tights lengthen her leg under a midi.

looks.comment: This is the true 'surprise me' look. It turns a once-worn evening slip and a once-worn tweed jacket into a Ganni and Rixo daytime look with arm coverage, and the cropped jacket marks her waist. The black tights and knee-high boots (m88, m67) give her a long unbroken leg.

failures.detail: Her go-to leopard blouse (m01) with mustard and burgundy is a textbook autumn palette, not something she 'wouldn't normally think of'. It is the weakest answer to this brief.

Pleated A-line midi (m21), a longline cardigan (m41) and a mid-length navy puffer (m53) over flat ankle boots stack volume on a short-legged frame. That is exactly the swamped feeling of her known tulle and cable-knit miss, and the belt gets buried under the puffer.
She finds the puffer (m53) dull, and it kills the look the moment she steps outside. The camel coat (m50) is warm enough for 9°C drizzle and keeps the warm story intact.

looks.comment: The colours flatter her, but the outfit is matchy (beret m87 echoing cardigan m41) and predictable. The puffer adds the volume problem the stylist claims the belt solves.

judgement.missedOpportunity: Replace Look 3 with a genuinely unexpected one: m02 emerald puff-sleeve poplin blouse tucked into m21 mustard pleated midi, cinched with m85, plus m88 tights and m67 flat knee-high boots. Finish with m83 resin flower earrings (worn once), m74 red mini bag and m50 camel coat. It is emerald-on-saffron colour-blocking with a romantic sleeve and a sharp boot, and it uses three under-worn pieces.
judgement.summary: Two strong looks and one filler. Look 1 finally gives the never-worn check blazer a convincing, polished print-mix. Look 2 is the real surprise: velvet slip, silk shirt and pink boucle, worth sending with a note on tucking the shirt smoothly. Look 3 answers 'surprise me' with her usual leopard blouse in a predictable autumn palette. It also stacks volume under a puffer she dislikes. The weather handling and directives (no suede in rain, arms covered, flats) are solid throughout. Swap Look 3 for something that uses the emerald blouse or the resin earrings before this goes out.

results.requestText: It's raining all day and I'll be walking a lot. What should I wear?

looks.title: Baroque in the Rain
looks.idea: Her gallery-opening dress, made weatherproof with flat knee-high boots and a belted trench.
looks.howToWear: Wear the wrap dress with black opaque tights and flat knee-high boots, so the midi hem skims the boot tops and no wet leg shows. Belt the trench at the natural waist over the wrap to keep her hourglass line. Turn the trench collar up against the breeze. Add the gold hoops and a few bangles pushed up the wrist. Wear the tan crossbody under the coat so her hands stay free for walking and an umbrella.
looks.why: It repeats what worked for her: the baroque wrap, a defined waist and gold hoops. The long sleeves cover her arms, and flat boots under a midi are dry and easy to walk in. The trench keeps it polished, and the burgundy, gold and navy print is warm and flattering. It avoids the black-blazer-over-colour problem because the print is the focus.

looks.title: Emerald and Navy, Cropped for Puddles
looks.idea: A crisp colour-on-colour pitch-ready look with a cinched waist and ankle-skimming trousers.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the puff-sleeve emerald blouse neatly into the navy cropped trousers and cinch with the wide black belt to mark the waist. The cropped hem sits above the ankle rain boots, so nothing drags in puddles. Wear the trench open or belted over the top. Add the gold hoops and carry the red mini bag as the sharp pop of colour.
looks.why: Emerald and navy is a rich, warm-leaning pairing in the spirit of her cobalt-and-navy joy look. The structured puff sleeves cover her arms and add the romantic edge with polish. Cropped trousers are the sensible rain choice because they keep hems dry, and the belted high waist suits her proportions. The trench repeats from look one because it is her only polished waterproof layer. If this is a pitch day, swap the rain boots for the Chelsea boots once you arrive.

looks.title: Mustard and Cobalt Puffer Day
looks.idea: A joyful colour-blocked walking outfit that makes the practical puffer feel intentional.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the fine cobalt merino into the high-waisted mustard pleated skirt so the waist stays marked. Wear black opaque tights and the ankle rain boots. Zip the navy puffer over the top. Knot the silk floral scarf at the neck so its rust, navy and cream tones show at the collar. Add the burgundy beret and gold hoops. Carry the tan crossbody under the puffer or across your body over it.
looks.why: Cobalt and mustard are both warm brights that flatter her. The fine merino keeps her from feeling swamped, which was the problem with the cream jumper and tulle skirt. The scarf adds a print and a romantic touch, and the beret lifts the puffer she finds dull. It is the warmest and most practical option for a long walk in steady rain at 8°C.

output.note: Her only genuinely waterproof, polished layer is the black trench, so it appears in two looks. The navy puffer is the second weather-proof option. I left out the suede boots, the patent flats and the full-length wide-leg trousers because their hems and finishes would be ruined in all-day rain.

failures.detail: Turning the black trench m51 collar up puts stark black right at her face. The silk floral scarf m84 (rust/navy/cream) was available to break it and add a second print.
Silky jersey m30 under cotton gabardine m51 (warmth 3) is on the cool side for a breezy 8°C walking day. A warmer under-layer or the scarf would help.
This is her proven gallery look with the weather pieces swapped in. There is no print-mixing and no new idea.

looks.comment: A sensible, flattering way to rain-proof her best-loved m30: knee boots m67 over 60-denier tights m88 keep her legs dry, and belting the trench at the waist holds the hourglass. It needed m84 at the neck to soften the head-to-toe black outer shell and to bring in her print-mixing signature.

failures.detail: Cotton poplin m02 (warmth 2), stretch-cotton trousers m27 (warmth 2) and a cotton gabardine trench m51 (warmth 3) are too little for a full day walking at 8°C in wind and steady rain. There is no knit layer, though m10 or m41 was available.
Cropped cigarette trousers m27 meeting ankle rain boots m69 cut her already-short leg line twice. The structured puff sleeves of m02 will also be crushed inside the trench sleeves.
The advice to swap into Chelsea boots on arrival means carrying a second pair of boots, but the only bag is the tiny red mini m74, which cannot hold them.
There is no print anywhere for a print-led client. The look is solid emerald, navy and black with black accessories, which edges toward the corporate feel she rejects.
It calls navy 'warm-leaning', which it is not. It also cites the cobalt/navy-floral look as precedent while dropping the print that made that look joyful.

looks.comment: The colour idea is fine, but this is a cold, cotton-only outfit for an all-day downpour. The rubber rain boots undercut the 'pitch-ready' promise, and the plan to change shoes has nowhere to carry them.

failures.detail: The crepe pleats of m21 will hang below the puffer m53 and go limp when soaked. A wool beret m87 in steady rain is warm but will get wet.

looks.comment: This is the real answer to the brief. Fine cobalt merino m10 tucked into high-waisted mustard m21 keeps the waist, and tights with rain boots keep her legs dry and warm. The m84 scarf and m87 beret turn the puffer she finds dull into a deliberate, Susie Lau-style colour clash. The most joyful and genuinely weatherproof look of the three.

judgement.missedOpportunity: Her proven Friday formula, rain-proofed: leopard silk blouse m01 tucked into high-rise jeans m24, black Chelsea boots m60 (leather, flat, dry), black trench m51 belted, silk floral scarf m84 at the neck for a leopard-and-floral print mix and warm colour at the face, gold hoops m80, and the black tote m71 big enough for the day. Add the burgundy longline cardigan m41 under the trench for warmth. This would replace Look 2 with something warm, walkable, polished and unmistakably her.
judgement.summary: Look 3 is the strongest: warm, waterproof, colour-forward and clearly her. Look 1 is a sound, flattering rain adaptation of her signature dress, but it misses the scarf that would fix black at the face and add a second print. Look 2 should not go out. It is too cold for 8°C with wind and rain, it shortens her leg line, it has no print, and its shoe-swap advice is impossible with a mini bag. The rain thinking is good: excluding the suede boots m61, the patent flats m62 and the floor-length wide-legs was correct. Overall, two of the three looks are usable, but the wardrobe's print-mixing potential is barely touched.

results.requestText: First date — cocktails at a smart bar.

looks.title: Baroque Wrap, Date-Night Edit
looks.idea: Her proven baroque wrap, sharpened with kitten heels and a red pop so it reads romantic and confident.
looks.howToWear: Wrap the dress snugly so the tie sits at the narrowest point of your waist. Add sheer-feeling black tights and the 4cm slingbacks. Wear the gold hoops and the bangle stack on one wrist only. Carry the red mini bag as the single sharp accent. Wear the camel coat open so the wrap neckline and waist show, and belt it only for the walk.
looks.why: The baroque wrap is her most complimented outfit and it is warm, long-sleeved and flattering on an hourglass shape. Burgundy, gold and navy suit her warm colouring. The black stays low at the legs and feet, away from her face. The 4cm heel is well under her 7cm limit and fine for the Tube. Leather shoes are the safer choice in drizzle than suede.

looks.title: Emerald Velvet, Tweed Twist
looks.idea: Jewel-toned velvet with a pink tweed jacket: romantic, slightly unexpected, and still polished.
looks.howToWear: Wear the slip dress with the cropped tweed jacket left open. It stops at the waist and keeps your proportions defined. Add black opaque tights and the flat knee-high boots so the hem and boot top overlap and make one long line. Wear the pearl drops and leave your neck bare. Carry the beaded clutch. Put the belted trench over everything for the drizzle and take it off at the bar.
looks.why: Emerald is one of her best colours. Pink against green is a joyful, Dries-Van-Noten-style pairing, and the bias-cut velvet is sleek on her waist. The tweed adds the one sharp, textured element and covers her shoulders. This look uses two under-worn pieces, and it avoids the black-blazer-over-party-dress mistake. The water-resistant trench and flat boots suit a wet walk.

looks.title: Check Blazer, Gold Camisole
looks.idea: A sharp, slightly undone tailoring look in warm autumn tones, with satin underneath for date-night heat.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the gold camisole into the navy cropped trousers. Add the wide black belt at the waist, with the blazer left open so the belt shows. Push the blazer sleeves up to the forearm. Wear the red Mary Janes and carry the red mini bag so the red repeats. Add the gold hoops and the bangles. Wear the camel coat over the top for the walk.
looks.why: This finally gives the unworn oversized check blazer a partner. The slim, cropped trousers balance the blazer's volume, so she isn't swamped. The belt keeps her waist defined. Gold, navy, rust and red sit well with her warm colouring. The red patent flats worked before with navy and are wet-weather friendly. The look is eclectic and relaxed without being casual.

output.note: I left out the tan suede boots because of the drizzle, and I kept the black blazer out of the mix so the looks stay colourful. Everything here is flat or under 5cm for the walk and Tube.

failures.detail: This is essentially her proven gallery look (m30 + m80) with the m61 boots swapped for m65 kitten heels. It is right for the date but adds no new idea and no print-mixing, even though she is print-led.

It calls the tights 'sheer-feeling', but m88 is 60 denier opaque. It also never checks whether the red m74 sits well against the burgundy in m30, which is the one colour relationship that needed justifying.
Slingbacks over opaque nylon tend to slip when walking. The m50 wool coat is not water-resistant, so it is fine in light drizzle but not ideal.

looks.comment: This is a dependable, flattering first-date answer that marks the waist, keeps her warm and keeps black low and away from her face. It is safe rather than inspired. Adding m84 knotted at the bag strap, or m66 leopard loafers, would have given her the print-on-print signature.

failures.detail: At 9°C with drizzle, a velvet slip (m38) under a waist-cropped boucle jacket (m42) and an unlined cotton trench (m51, warmth 3) will feel cool on the walk, even though the bar itself will be warm.
The textures stack up: velvet, boucle and the multicolour beaded clutch m73 (formality 5) compete with the pink-on-emerald story. The red m74 or tan m70 would let the colour pairing lead.

looks.comment: Emerald velvet with pink tweed is a genuinely joyful, Dries-like colour move, and it brings two under-worn pieces into play. Tweed with pearls tips slightly ladylike rather than eclectic. Chunky hoops (m80) would keep it more Maya.

failures.detail: Her legs are short relative to her torso. The hip-length oversized blazer (m45) cuts her at the hip, the ankle-cropped m27 cuts her again at the ankle, and the contrasting flat red m62 shortens the leg line further.
The wide black belt m85 is the only black in a brown, rust, gold, navy and red palette, so it reads as an orphan. The matching red shoes and bag also feel matchy rather than intentional.
Bare ankles in cropped stretch-cotton trousers and patent flats are chilly for a 9°C drizzly evening. Layering the m50 coat over an oversized wool blazer will also be bulky.
It claims the slim cropped trousers 'balance' the blazer but ignores her leg-to-torso ratio, which is the key fit fact for this client.

looks.comment: Finding a partner for the unworn m45 is the right instinct, but the navy office cigarette trousers make it feel like a work look and shorten her line. The obvious partner for a large check is a high-rise, full-length floral, which is her print-mixing sweet spot.

judgement.missedOpportunity: m45 oversized check blazer worn open over m03 gold satin camisole tucked into m20 navy floral high-rise wide-leg trousers (check-on-floral print-mixing, with the full-length wide leg lengthening her line). Finish with m65 kitten heels peeking out, m80 hoops and m82 bangles, the m74 red mini bag, and m51 trench for the drizzle.
judgement.summary: These are competent, wearable looks that respect her heel, colour and wet-weather limits. Looks 1 and 2 could go out with minor tweaks. However, for a print-led, eclectic client, none of the three looks actually mixes prints, which is the core of her Style DNA. Look 3 wastes the check blazer on office trousers with a leg-shortening crop. The strongest idea here is the emerald-and-pink colour play. The best possible answer, check blazer over floral wide-legs, was left on the table.

results.requestText: Weekend brunch and then wandering around the shops.

looks.title: The Blazer Finally Gets Its Moment
looks.idea: A rust-and-cream check boyfriend blazer over cobalt and denim, with a silk scarf tying the colours together.
looks.howToWear: Wear the cobalt merino tucked into the high-rise jeans so your waist shows under the oversized blazer. Roll the blazer sleeves to the forearm and roll the jean hem once for a clean ankle. Knot the silk scarf loosely at the neck, with the rust showing against the cobalt. Tilt the burgundy beret back off your forehead for drizzle cover, and sling the tan crossbody across the body so it doesn't fight the blazer's volume.
looks.why: This puts the unworn blazer with the cobalt and jeans you already wear and love. Cobalt is one of your best colours and it sits at your face. The fitted tucked top under the roomy blazer avoids the swamped top-and-bottom volume that didn't work before. Brown and rust check against cobalt and a floral scarf is print-mixing with a bit of polish, and leather trainers are comfortable for hours of shopping.

looks.title: Mustard, Navy and a Little Romance
looks.idea: A pleated mustard midi with a Breton stripe, finished with a belted trench and a pop of red.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the Breton top fully into the high-waisted pleated skirt and let the trench hang open. Belt the trench if the drizzle picks up. Wear the black tights with the flat knee-high boots, so the skirt hem sits just above the boot tops. Tie the silk scarf at the bag strap or the neckline for the rust and navy. Wear the hoops and a few bangles, and carry the red mini bag on the shoulder.
looks.why: The mustard skirt marks your waist and the pleats move well when you walk. Mustard and navy stripes are warm and flattering, and they give you a joyful, slightly romantic look. The tights and the knee-high boots keep you warm and dry in 9° drizzle. The water-resistant trench gives the polish without a black blazer. The red bag is the one sharp element.

looks.title: Leopard Meets Floral
looks.idea: Two prints in a shared warm palette, with the waist belted and the camel coat wrapped over.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the leopard silk blouse into the high-rise floral wide-leg trousers, undo one more button than usual, and push the sleeves to three-quarter length. Add the wide black belt at the waist. The full-length trousers should skim the tops of the Chelsea boots. Wear the camel coat open over the top. Add the hoops and the stack of bangles, and wear the tan crossbody under the coat.
looks.why: This takes your Friday leopard blouse and pairs it with the floral trousers you've loved in colour-on-colour looks. The tan in the leopard picks up the camel coat, and the navy and pink floral stays calm against it. The belt and the high rise give your waist the definition you like, and the wide leg lengthens your legs. The wool coat and boots keep you warm and dry, and the look is easy to wear from brunch through the shops.

output.note: Everything here is leather or wool, so it holds up to light drizzle. I kept the suede block-heel boots and the calf-hair loafers out for that reason. You don't own an umbrella, so it may be worth taking one if the rain gets heavier.

failures.detail: At 9°C with drizzle and hours on foot, m45 over m10 is the only outer layer. Wool blazer plus fine merino is workable for short hops between shops, but it gets damp and chilly over a long afternoon. Either say plainly that it is a coat-free look for a milder hour, or suggest the m50 camel coat for the walk between brunch and the shops.

m63 white trainers are the comfortable default and flatten the joy. m62 red patent Mary Janes are just as walkable, drizzle-proof, and already proven with m10 in her colour-on-colour win. They would add the sharp element this look lacks.
m24 is already ankle length. Rolling it again cuts the leg higher on a short-legged 164cm frame, under a hip-length oversized blazer that already sits low. Leave the hem as is.

looks.comment: Finally activating the unworn m45 with cobalt m10 is exactly the right instinct. Rust/brown check against cobalt is a smart complementary pairing, and the m84 scarf adds a genuine second print. It needs a warmer outer plan for the weather and a less default shoe.

failures.detail: The legs are well covered with m88 and m67, but the top half is a thin cotton m06 under an unlined gabardine m51 (warmth 3). That is cool for a long, drizzly afternoon.

Breton, black trench, black tights and black knee boots is the stock Parisian formula. Three black pieces carry the outline, which edges toward the corporate black she dislikes. Only m21 and m74 bring her joy.

The romance in the title is never located. 'Tie the scarf at the bag strap or the neckline' is a non-decision. It should be the neckline, so the rust/navy floral sits between her face and the black trench collar.

looks.comment: Competent and weather-aware: the tonal black from tights to boots gives a continuous leg line under the m21 midi, and the red m74 is a clear accent. But it reads as a generic autumn uniform, not a sharper Maya, and the stripe-plus-floral mix is half-committed.

failures.detail: Full-length crepe wide-legs (m20) skimming m60 will wick drizzle and puddle water at the hem all afternoon. Mention it, or keep the hem just clear of the ground.

'Two prints in a shared warm palette' is inaccurate. m20 is navy/pink/green, which is cool-leaning, and m01 is tan/black/cream. The mix works because leopard behaves as a neutral and the black belt (m85) picks up m01's black, and that is the lesson she should hear. Both prints are also medium scale; it would help to note that the belt is what separates them.

looks.comment: The most on-DNA look of the three: it combines two of her proven pieces into a deliberate print clash. The waist is belted, the high rise does its job, and the camel m50 echoes the leopard's tan. It is warm and polished for brunch, and only the trouser hems need a real-life note.

judgement.missedOpportunity: The pink tweed cropped jacket m42 (worn once) is the piece most made for her proportions, because it stops at the waist and visually lengthens her legs. Wear it over the cobalt merino m10 tucked into the navy floral wide-legs m20, with the red patent Mary Janes m62 (drizzle-proof), red mini bag m74 and hoops m80, and the camel coat m50 on top for the walk. That takes her proven colour-on-colour win and adds a romantic, sharp texture. Notably, m62 went unused across all three looks.
judgement.summary: A solid, mostly sendable edit. Look 1 deserves credit for finally styling the unworn m45 with cobalt, and Look 3 is a confident leopard-and-floral mix that feels entirely like her. The stylist note is honest and useful about the suede and calf-hair pieces and the umbrella. Weaknesses: Look 1 has no proper outer layer for a 9°C drizzly afternoon on foot, and Look 2 leans on a safe Breton-and-black-trench formula. One explanation misdescribes the colour logic. The edit also leaves the best weather-proof joyful shoe (m62) and the waist-length pink tweed m42 on the hanger. It is competent with two good ideas; one more brave, proportion-smart look would have made it exceptional.

results.requestText: I'm presenting to senior leadership next week. I want to look authoritative but still like me.

looks.title: The Check Blazer, Finally
looks.idea: Tonal blues under a warm oversized check blazer: authority from tailoring, personality from colour.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the cobalt merino into the cigarette trousers and cinch it with the wide black belt so the waist reads under the oversized blazer. Wear the blazer open with the sleeves pushed up just once, so the cuff sits at the wrist and the shoulders stay slouchy. The cropped hem and Chelsea boots keep the leg line clean. Stack the bangles on one wrist and wear the hoops. The camel coat goes over the top for the Tube.
looks.why: The slim cropped trouser balances the oversized blazer, so you avoid the swamped volume that didn't work before. Cobalt next to rust and brown check is a warm, flattering mix, and it gives you the boardroom look in your own colours. It also finally puts m45 to work and avoids the corporate-black-blazer trap. Arms are covered and the flat boots can handle the drizzle.

looks.title: Baroque Authority
looks.idea: Your proven gallery-opening dress, sharpened for the boardroom with sleek flat boots and a trench.
looks.howToWear: Wear the wrap dress with the wrap tied snugly at the natural waist and the hem just above the top of the flat knee-high boots, with sheer-looking black tights where the hem and boot meet. Keep jewellery to the hoops and a few bangles so the print stays the star. Wear the belted trench cinched over the top for the commute and take it off in the room. Carry the black tote for your laptop.
looks.why: It marks your waist and has long sleeves, and the burgundy, gold and navy baroque print is rich and warm against your skin. It is the dress that has already made you feel completely like yourself, and the dark knee-high boot gives it the polish of a power look without adding a blazer. The water-resistant trench handles the drizzle and the flat boots work for the walking.

looks.title: Emerald Command
looks.idea: Sharp black tailoring with a saturated emerald top: decisive, a bit romantic, unmistakably yours.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the crisp puff-sleeve blouse into the high-rise wide-leg trousers and add the wide belt over the blouse to define the waist. Let the trousers skim the floor over the kitten heels to lengthen your legs. Keep the gold hoops and bangles. Wear the camel coat on the commute, and put the heels on at the office if the pavements are slick.
looks.why: The black trousers are your most authoritative piece, and emerald is one of your flattering warm brights, so the black sits away from your face and doesn't drain you. The puff sleeves are the romantic edge and the sharp crease is the polish. The high rise and belt mark your waist, the 4cm heel keeps within your limit, and the arms are covered.

output.note: The black blazer is deliberately left out. For this pitch the check blazer, baroque dress and emerald blouse give polish with more personality. If you want a fourth option, the ivory silk shirt with the black trousers and pink tweed jacket would be a softer version.

failures.detail: m45 is an oversized, hip-length boyfriend blazer worn open, so it covers the m85 belt and ends at her widest point. On a short-legged hourglass the 'tuck and belt' move mostly disappears. The cropped m27 hem also shortens the leg further. A half-tuck with the blazer pushed back, or a cropped-waist jacket, would actually show the waist.

The black belt (m85) and black Chelsea boots (m60) sit against a brown/rust/cream check and navy trousers with nothing tying them together. Tan suede boots (m61) or the leopard loafers (m66) would pick up the check, and m66 could go into the bag for indoors.

Calling it 'tonal blues' turns a print-led client into solids-plus-one-check. The rust/navy/cream silk scarf (m84) is the obvious bridge between the check and the navy and would give her the intentional print mix.
'Push the sleeves up just once so the cuff sits at the wrist' is confusing. The note also doesn't address bulk from tucking a crew-neck merino jumper.

looks.comment: Putting m45 to work with cobalt is a smart, warm colour idea, and it is the most 'authoritative-yet-hers' concept on the page. The execution is let down by a hidden belt, black accents that muddy the brown check, and no print mix. Add m84 at the neck and swap to m61 or m66 and it becomes a strong look.

failures.detail: The note asks for 'sheer-looking black tights' but m88 is 60-denier opaque. That is the right choice for 9°C, but the description is wrong.

This is essentially the proven gallery outfit (m30) with darker boots. Its claim to boardroom authority is thin: there is no sharp structured element in the room once the trench comes off, and the client's own formula asks for 'one sharp element'.

looks.comment: Reliable, flattering and practical. The wrap marks the waist, the sleeves are long, and m88 with m67 gives an unbroken dark leg that helps her proportions, while m51 handles the drizzle. It is the safest yes rather than an evolution toward 'polished at pitches', and it needed one structured or sharp accent to feel like a power look.

failures.detail: The trousers are hemmed to skim the floor over kitten heels, and she is told to change into the heels at the office. No commute shoe is named. In a flat, those hems will drag through wet pavements, and leather slingbacks (m65) are a poor drizzle shoe in their own right.

Solid emerald over solid black is colour-blocking, not print-led. It is the look most likely to read as 'generic smart creative'. The leopard loafers (m66) or the m84 scarf at the neck would put her signature back in.
There is no commute shoe, and every accent is black (m85, m65, m71). The look has nothing that reads as Maya beyond the colour of the blouse.

looks.comment: Proportionally the soundest look. The high-rise crease-front m23 with a tucked, belted m02 marks the waist and lengthens the leg, and the puff sleeve against the sharp crease is a real romantic-plus-sharp tension. It just stops short of her print DNA and leaves the wet commute unsolved.

judgement.missedOpportunity: The pink tweed cropped jacket (m42, worn once) is the pitch-polish piece this wardrobe was built for. It is boxy, cropped at the waist and Chanel-coded, so it gives authority while marking her waist and lengthening her leg, which the oversized m45 cannot do. Pair it with the m13 ivory silk shirt tucked into the high-rise m20 navy floral wide-leg trousers, add m61 tan block-heel boots or the m62 red Mary Janes (the latter if the drizzle stops; the 5cm block on m61 is within her limit), plus m80 hoops and m70 crossbody, under the m51 trench. That is a print-led, colour-forward suit equivalent that is unmistakably her and clearly senior. A close second is m45 over the m01 leopard blouse with m23 black wide-leg trousers and m66 loafers, a check-with-leopard mix that shares tan, rust and cream.
judgement.summary: A competent, safe set of three that correctly avoids the black-blazer trap and respects every directive (arms covered, heels ≤7cm, nothing strapless). It finally gives the unworn check blazer a job. But the brief was 'authoritative but still like me', and two of the three looks drop her print-mixing identity for solids, while the third repeats the gallery outfit. Specific fixes: Look 1's belt disappears under the open oversized blazer and its black accents muddy the brown check (add m84 and m61/m66). Look 3 needs a named commute shoe and a hem plan for the wet. The strongest polish-with-personality option, the waist-cropped pink tweed jacket over the floral wide-leg trousers, was pushed into a throwaway 'fourth option' paired with plain black trousers instead.

results.requestText: Wedding guest — outdoor afternoon ceremony, and the forecast says it might rain.

looks.title: Baroque and Belt
looks.idea: Your most proven romantic print, made rain-proof with flat knee boots and a belted trench.
looks.howToWear: Wear the wrap dress with the waist tie pulled snug so the defined waist is the focus. Add black opaque tights under flat knee-high boots, which are steady on wet grass. Belt the trench over the dress at the same height as the wrap, cinching it so the waist reads twice. Keep the tan crossbody across the body for hands-free umbrella duty. Chunky hoops are the only jewellery needed, since the print carries the look.
looks.why: This is the spirit of your gallery-opening dress, which got the compliments. It has long sleeves, a defined waist and a midi length that suits your proportions. The flat boots and water-resistant trench handle drizzle and a lawn. The burgundy, gold and navy print is rich and warm against your colouring, and nothing black sits at your face.

looks.title: Velvet and Tweed
looks.idea: Emerald velvet with a pink tweed jacket: joyful, romantic, one sharp waist-cropped edge.
looks.howToWear: Put the velvet slip on with the cropped tweed jacket buttoned or just closed at the waist, so the jacket's hem sits at your narrowest point and the bias skirt falls from there. The jacket covers your arms and stops the slip from feeling bare in November. Add black tights and flat Chelsea boots, with the hem skimming the boot tops. Wear small pearl drops and carry the beaded clutch. Put the camel coat over the top for the walk in and take it off for photos.
looks.why: Emerald is one of your strongest colours and pink gives it a warm, romantic lift. The tweed jacket is under-worn and finishes the dress with a sharp, polished element, without the corporate feel of the black blazer. Flat boots keep you safe on damp ground. The beaded clutch brings in multicolour to link the pink and green.

looks.title: Mustard, Emerald, Red
looks.idea: Warm brights stacked on purpose: crisp emerald sleeves over a pleated mustard midi, with a red pop.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the boxy poplin blouse fully into the high-waisted pleated skirt so the waist is clean and defined, and let the puff sleeves be the statement. Wear black opaque tights with the red patent Mary Janes. Patent wipes clean and flats are good on grass. Add hoops and a couple of bangles, and carry the red mini bag so it matches your shoes. Wear the camel coat open over the top, which keeps the look warm-toned.
looks.why: This is colour-on-colour in the way that felt joyful before, and every piece is a warm bright that flatters you. The puff sleeves cover your arms, and the high-rise pleated skirt balances your short legs and torso. Two under-worn pieces (the blouse and the skirt) get used, and the red accents add personality while the look stays polished enough for a wedding.

output.note: Your wardrobe has no umbrella, so bring one. I kept the tan suede boots and the leopard faux-fur coat out of the forecast drizzle. I also avoided the mint blouse, which drains you, and the powder blue tulle skirt, which has already overwhelmed you. Mid-blue jeans and the cobalt jumper are too casual for a ceremony. Two coats cover three looks, so the camel coat appears twice.

failures.detail: The note claims 'nothing black sits at your face', but closed and belted for drizzle, the m51 black trench collar frames her face all through the ceremony. Her profile flags stark black at the face as draining.

m84 silk floral scarf (rust/navy/cream) knotted at the trench neck would warm the face, echo the m30 navy, and add a deliberate print-mix. Without it the outdoor view is black coat, black tights and black boots.
This is a weatherproofed repeat of her proven gallery look. The m70 tan everyday crossbody keeps it in daytime register for a wedding.

looks.comment: A sound, rain-ready answer built on m30, her most successful dress. The knee boots (m67) are the right call for wet grass. But with m51 belted shut, what guests see is mostly black, and an m84 scarf at the collar plus gold bangles (m82) would have made it feel like a wedding rather than a commute.

failures.detail: The m60 Chelsea boots read slightly casual against velvet and beading, and leave a skin-tight band of tights between hem and boot. m67 flat knee boots would give a longer, sleeker line under the midi, keep her legs drier, and suit her shorter legs better.
Camel wool (m50) isn't water-resistant, and velvet water-marks. Fine in light drizzle, but she should keep the coat on until under cover. A clutch plus an umbrella also leaves no free hand.

looks.comment: The strongest idea of the three: emerald velvet (m38) with the pink boucle (m42) is Gucci/Ganni colour play, it rescues two once-worn pieces, and the cropped jacket marks her waist. Swap m60 for m67 and consider m83 resin flower earrings over the rather proper pearls to push the joy.

failures.detail: Cotton poplin (m02) with a crepe pleated skirt (m21) is her office smart-casual, not wedding-guest dress. There is no fabric with occasion weight or sheen.
Low-cut patent flats (m62) over tights on a drizzly lawn mean wet, cold feet at 9°C. 'Patent wipes clean' doesn't address that.
Structured puff sleeves plus a pleated A-line skirt puts volume at both ends. That echoes her 'swamped' miss, only partly redeemed by the tuck.
The note calls red shoes plus red bag a match, as if that were a virtue, but it reads dated rather than intentional. It also ignores how thin the layers are under the coat outdoors.

looks.comment: Joyful colour logic that's true to her colour-on-colour win. But it's a creative-office outfit, not a wedding one, and the flats are wrong for a wet lawn.

judgement.missedOpportunity: Her DNA is print-led and print-mixing, yet no look mixes prints. The best missed answer: m30 baroque wrap dress + m84 silk floral scarf knotted at the neck of m51 trench (print-on-print, warm at the face) + m67 knee boots + m88 tights + m80 hoops + m82 bangles + m73 beaded clutch. Alternatively, m45 check blazer (worn 0x, rust/brown) as the sharp layer over m38 velvet.
judgement.summary: A thoughtful, weather-aware set that respects every directive, sensibly keeps the suede boots and faux fur out of the rain, and wakes up several under-worn pieces. Look 2 is the standout. Look 1 is reliable but needs the black-at-the-face problem fixed with m84. Look 3 is under-dressed for a wedding and wet-footed. The bigger miss is identity: a print-mixing client gets no print-mixing, and the never-worn m45 check blazer is left on the rail.

results.requestText: How should I wear my oversized check blazer (m45)?

looks.title: Colour-on-Colour with a Check Twist
looks.idea: Your joyful cobalt-and-navy-floral combination, with the check blazer as the sharp, grown-up layer.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the cobalt merino into the high-rise floral trousers so the waist shows, and let the hems skim the tops of the Mary Janes. Wear the blazer open with the sleeves pushed up once, to show the wrist and keep the shape from swamping you. Keep the jewellery to the gold hoops. Wear the black trench over everything for the drizzle and carry the tan crossbody.
looks.why: This is the formula that already worked for you: colour-on-colour with red patent flats. The rust in the check picks up the pink in the floral, and the cobalt cuts through the warm browns. The blazer adds polish for the office without the corporate feel of your black one. High-rise trousers and a tucked-in knit keep the oversized blazer from hiding your waist.

looks.title: Pitch-Day Pleats
looks.idea: Warm, autumnal tailoring where a silk scarf ties the check and the mustard together.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the ivory silk shirt into the mustard pleated skirt. Knot the rust, navy and cream scarf loosely at the collar, with the shirt's top button open. Put the blazer on and belt it at the natural waist with the wide black belt, so the oversized shape gets an hourglass. Add black opaque tights and the flat knee-high boots, which also cope with the wet pavements. Put the camel coat over the top for the commute.
looks.why: Belting the blazer marks your waist and turns a boyfriend cut into something deliberate and polished, which suits a client pitch. Mustard, rust and ivory are warm and flattering on you, and the scarf repeats the check's colours so the print mix looks planned. Your arms are covered, there are no heels, and it stays colourful and a little romantic with the pleats and silk.

looks.title: Velvet and Check After Dark
looks.idea: A romantic emerald slip with a slouchy check blazer thrown over it, for dinner or a gallery opening.
looks.howToWear: Wear the emerald velvet slip as the base and drape the blazer over it, either open or with the shoulders slightly slipped off. Roll the sleeves to the forearm so the bangles show. Add black opaque tights and the Chelsea boots to take the sweetness down a notch. Carry the red mini bag for a tomato pop against the emerald. Add the gold hoops and bangle stack, and wear the trench belted over the top for the walk and the drizzle.
looks.why: Emerald is one of your best colours, and the rust-brown check sits well with it. The slip gives the romantic element and the oversized blazer gives the sharp one, which is your Style DNA. The blazer also covers your arms, since the slip has thin straps. Flat boots keep it comfortable on the Tube and in the rain, and the red bag finishes it without the black-blazer-over-red problem, because this blazer is warm rather than corporate.

output.note: Every look uses the check blazer (m45), as you asked, with a different anchor piece in each so you get three different ways to wear it. Avoid the tan suede boots in this drizzle, and the Breton top or leopard blouse with jeans would also work under it for a weekend. The blazer pairs best with solid or small-scale pieces in warm brights, and it has no formal black to fall back on, which is the point.

failures.detail: Red patent Mary Janes (m62) leave the ankles bare at 9°C in drizzle, and full-length crepe wide-legs (m20) will wick up wet pavement. Patent copes with the rain, but tan-free Chelsea boots (m60) under the hems would be warmer on a drizzly day.

An oversized boyfriend blazer (m45) under a belted, knee-length gabardine trench (m51) is likely to bunch at the shoulders and sleeves. Tell her to check the fit, or to carry the trench rather than belt it.
A hip-length oversized blazer over full wide-legs shortens legs that are already short. It only works because the knit is tucked and the blazer stays open, so that move must be non-negotiable.
'Rust picks up the pink in the floral' is a stretch. The real link is the cobalt/rust complementary contrast and the red shoe echoing the rust, and the explanation should say that.

looks.comment: Smart move to graft the new blazer onto her proven cobalt + navy floral + red Mary Jane formula (m10/m20/m62). The large check against the medium floral is a genuine print-mix at a different scale, very Dries. It is a little reliant on the known hit, but it gives her a real office answer straight away.

failures.detail: For a client pitch, the compact tan crossbody (m70) won't hold a laptop or pitch materials. The black leather tote (m71) is the working bag here, and its black ties to the belt and boots.
The knotted scarf (m84), the blazer lapels and the camel coat collar are a lot of layers at the neck. Suggest she wears the scarf inside the open shirt collar so the neck stays clean.

looks.comment: This is the strongest answer to her stated aspiration. Belting the boyfriend blazer with m85 over the mustard pleats (m21) gives her the waist and real pitch polish. The scarf (m84) repeats the check's rust, navy and cream so the print mix reads as planned. Flat knee boots (m67) with tights (m88) are right for the wet and keep the lower leg a continuous line. It leans autumnal-tonal rather than joyful, but mustard keeps it from going beige.

failures.detail: A bias-cut slip (m38) with a slouchy open boyfriend blazer (m45) gives her hourglass no waist at all. She prefers outfits that mark the waist. Belting the trench helps only on the walk; indoors she's a straight column under a boxy jacket.

Her only layers are a thin-strap velvet slip, a blazer and a warmth-3 trench (m51) at 9°C in drizzle for an evening out, so she will be cold on the walk home. The 'shoulders slipped off' move is not realistic in this weather.
An oversized blazer squeezed under a belted trench will crush the very slouch the look depends on.

The note about the black-blazer-over-red problem is irrelevant here. The real colour logic goes unexplained: rust against emerald as complements, and whether tomato (m74) plus emerald plus rust check needs the gold to bridge them.

looks.comment: A lovely romantic-plus-sharp concept that gets the rarely worn velvet slip (m38) out. But it loses her waist, and the outerwear is a weak, cold choice for an evening. The leopard faux-fur coat (m52) over check and emerald would have been warmer and far more Michele, which is exactly the eclectic clash her DNA wants. Alternatively, the wide belt over the blazer would at least restore her shape.

judgement.missedOpportunity: A weekend market look: m01 leopard silk blouse + m45 check blazer + m24 mid-blue jeans (high-rise, blouse tucked) + m60 Chelsea boots + m87 burgundy beret + m80 hoops + m70 crossbody, with m52 leopard faux-fur coat or m53 puffer for the drizzle. It builds on her proven Friday formula and adds a leopard-and-check animal-meets-heritage print clash. The stylist only mentioned it in passing in the note. Alternatively, m52 should have replaced m51 in Look 3.
judgement.summary: A thoughtful, usable answer to 'how do I wear this?'. It gives three distinct jobs (office, pitch, evening), all directive-safe, and each uses a different anchor. Look 2 is the standout: belting the blazer delivers the polish she wants at pitches without going corporate. Look 1 smartly leans on a proven combination. Look 3 has the most romantic idea but the weakest execution: no waist, a cold, cramped trench over the blazer, and thin reasoning. The repeated choice of the slim black trench over an oversized jacket is a practical blind spot. The leopard faux-fur coat (m52), the black tote for pitch days, and a proper weekend look were all left on the table.

results.requestText: Long travel day tomorrow — I want to be comfortable but still look put-together.

looks.title: Camel & Cobalt Traveller
looks.idea: Colour-on-colour warmth with a printed silk scarf as the one sharp, romantic touch.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the cobalt merino into the high-rise corduroy flares so the waist stays marked and the flare lengthens your leg line. Wear the flares over the Chelsea boots so only the toe shows. Knot the rust, navy and cream silk scarf loosely at the neck, with the tails tucked into the jumper. Belt the trench at the waist and wear the crossbody across your body so your hands are free. Add the gold hoops.
looks.why: Cobalt and camel are the same warm-neutral and warm-bright pairing she loves, and it echoes her navy and cobalt colour-on-colour look. Everything is soft and stretchy enough for hours of sitting. Corduroy and merino are warm on a cold plane, and the Chelsea boots and water-resistant trench cope with drizzle. The scarf keeps it from reading as a plain travel uniform.

looks.title: Print-on-Print Easy Layers
looks.idea: Stripe meets floral in a shared navy, softened with burgundy and finished with a camel coat.
looks.howToWear: Tuck the Breton top into the high-rise navy floral wide-legs so the waist is clear and the trousers skim the white trainers. Layer the burgundy longline cardigan open over the top, so it adds a vertical line and sits easily on a plane. Wear the camel coat open over the top and carry the tote. Add the hoops and the gold bangle stack.
looks.why: The navy runs through both prints, so the mix looks intentional rather than busy. The burgundy picks up the colour in the floral. It's the most comfortable look of the three: crepe trousers, cotton jersey and trainers made for walking. The layers come off easily when the Tube or the terminal is warm, and the camel coat makes it look polished rather than sporty.

looks.title: Baroque Wrap, Travel-Ready
looks.idea: Her most flattering print dress, made practical with tights, flat boots and a beret.
looks.howToWear: Wear the baroque wrap dress with the black opaque tights and flat knee-high boots, so the line from hem to boot is continuous. Tie the wrap snugly at the waist. Set the burgundy beret slightly back on the head and add the hoops and bangles. Wear the navy puffer open or zipped over the top, and carry the tote.
looks.why: The wrap dress is a proven winner for her. It marks the waist, has long sleeves and stretches in silky jersey, so it's as comfy as a loungewear piece. Tights and tall flat boots keep her warm and dry. The beret picks up the burgundy in the print, and the navy puffer echoes the navy in the dress, so the practical coat looks chosen. The one compromise is that the puffer is her least favourite piece, but it's the best choice for a wet, cold travel day.

output.note: I left out the black blazer, mint blouse and powder-blue skirt. They don't suit her colouring or the day, and the blazer is her usual default. The oversized check blazer would be bulky over everything else for a long journey, so it's better saved for an office day. Pack a spare layer, such as the burgundy cardigan, in your tote because planes and trains can be cold.

failures.detail: For a print-led, eclectic client the only print is a small square scarf (m84). The look is solid cobalt and camel under a black trench (m51). It is well judged but reads more 'nice travel outfit' than Maya.
The compact tan crossbody (m70) is too small to be the only bag on a long travel day. Pair it with the black tote (m71) for snacks, a charger and the spare layer the note itself recommends.

It calls the look 'soft and stretchy enough for hours of sitting', but corduroy flares (m26) worn high-rise with a tuck are not stretchy. The note should acknowledge the waistband or suggest an untucked front-tuck for the seated hours.

looks.comment: A solid, weather-ready look: the tucked cobalt merino (m10) into high-rise camel flares (m26) marks the waist and lengthens the leg, and the belted trench (m51) handles drizzle. It just plays her colour-on-colour card without much of her print appetite. A leopard collar (m01) under the merino would have made it hers.

failures.detail: Three long lines stack up: full-length wide-legs (m20), an open longline cardigan (m41) and a below-knee coat (m50). Together they swallow the waist the tuck was meant to show and shorten her already short leg line. The cardigan should be packed, not worn.

Full-length crepe wide-legs over flat white trainers (m63) will wick drizzle at the hem all day. The camel wool coat (m50) is the one non-water-resistant coat here. Chelsea boots (m60) and the trench (m51) would make it travel-proof.

It claims the burgundy 'picks up the colour in the floral', but m20 is navy/pink/green, with no burgundy. The stylist's note also says to pack the burgundy cardigan as a spare when it is already worn in this look.
The bangle stack (m82) is a nuisance through airport or station security on a travel day.

looks.comment: The Breton (m06) and navy floral (m20) mix through a shared navy is the most 'Maya' idea in the set and genuinely comfortable. Over-layering and wet-hem trainers undo the polish, and the colour reasoning is invented. Fix it with m60, m51 belted, and m41 in the tote.

failures.detail: The navy puffer (m53) is the warmest, most practical coat but the one she finds dull. At 9°C over tights and boots, the belted black trench (m51) would keep the waist and the polish and still shed drizzle. The trade-off is honestly flagged, though.

looks.comment: Translating her proven gallery dress (m30) into travel mode works well. Opaque tights (m88) and flat knee-highs (m67) tucked under the midi hem give a long, warm, dry line, and the burgundy beret (m87) is a nice finishing move. The stylist was right to say plainly that the puffer is a compromise.

judgement.missedOpportunity: Wear the leopard silk blouse (m01) with its collar and cuffs out under the cobalt merino (m10). Tuck it into the camel corduroy flares (m26) and finish with the black Chelsea boots (m60), the belted black trench (m51), the black tote (m71) and the gold hoops (m80). That gives the warmth and drizzle-proofing of Look 1 plus her signature leopard-and-colour mix, which is the print-led sharpness that Look 1 lacks.
judgement.summary: A sensible, weather-aware set with genuine range: solid colour-on-colour, print-on-print and her hero dress. Look 3 is the standout. Look 1 is safe but sendable. Look 2 has the most personality but is over-layered, impractical at the hem in drizzle, and justified with a colour claim that isn't true (there is no burgundy in m20). The note also contradicts Look 2 by suggesting the burgundy cardigan be packed when it is already being worn. For a print-led client, more of her print vocabulary (m01, m66) could have reached the travel looks. Tighten Look 2 before sending.

results.requestText: What should I wear to work tomorrow?

looks.title: Earth and Green
looks.idea: Warm, tonal texture in forest green and chocolate, which is the colour he's been missing, and still quiet.
looks.howToWear: Wear the forest green merino with its hem left out over the chocolate cords, with the sleeves pushed to mid-forearm. Cuff the cords once, just above the lug boots, so the boot shape shows and the hem stays clear of the chain. Put the olive waxed jacket over the top with the corduroy collar up for the wind, and tuck the navy scarf inside it. Brown belt, steel watch, and the roll-top backpack for the ride.
looks.why: The cords have only been worn twice because he wasn't sure what to wear them with. Forest green is in his palette and sits well against his cool colouring, and brown sits underneath it. The relaxed wide-wale cords are easy to pedal in, and the waxed jacket and rainproof lug boots handle the showers and wind. It is textural, warm and understated, with no navy-and-grey default.

looks.title: Soft Tailoring, Tonal Grey
looks.idea: His winter presentation formula, adapted to be rideable: the roll-neck and flannel, with a blazer in place of the overcoat.
looks.howToWear: Wear the charcoal roll-neck tucked loosely at the front only, so the flannel trousers keep a clean straight line. Layer the unlined navy blazer over it with the sleeves left at full length, which suits his long arms. Add the black belt to match the Chelsea boots. For the ride, wear the black rain shell over everything and take it off at the studio. The blazer stays dry and uncrushed underneath.
looks.why: This repeats the look that felt sharp at his last winter presentation, but swaps the knee-length overcoat for a blazer and a hip-length shell, which keeps it rideable. The lambswool, flannel and soft-shouldered blazer give plenty of texture. The Chelsea boots have a rubber sole for grip. It also works if a client drops in or a jacket is needed, and no tie is required.

looks.title: Rust Cord, Quietly
looks.idea: A muted rust corduroy shirt set against ecru and navy, so the colour reads as warmth rather than a statement.
looks.howToWear: Wear the rust cord shirt open at the collar over the ecru tee, so the ecru sits against his face and the rust stays further down. Leave the shirt untucked and roll the sleeves twice to the forearm. Tuck the tee into the navy pleated trousers under it. Wear the charcoal quilted liner under the black rain shell for the ride. Drape the navy scarf at the neck, which also keeps the rust off his face. Brown belt and steel watch.
looks.why: The rust shirt has only been worn twice, and here it adds the warmth he wants without sitting close to his face, where strong orange tones don't suit him. The navy pleated trousers are his dependable base and the brown derbies are his proven studio shoe, so it feels like his own style with one change. The liner and shell give wind and rain protection. The crepe-soled derbies are fine for a short ride, but suede can mark in a downpour, so swap to the lug boots if it is raining hard when you leave.

output.note: I've assumed a studio day with no client presentation, and that you are cycling. If you do have a presentation, Look 2 is the one to wear. I left out the camel suede trucker because of the showers, and the penny loafers because they are slippery on wet pedals.

failures.detail: The d65 belt is listed but the d12 hem is worn out over the cords, so it is invisible. No d63 beanie at 6°C in wind on a 25-minute ride.
The d41 jacket stops at the hip, so the wide-wale d26 thighs take the showers and corduroy soaks up water. Worth a word on drying them off or keeping the shell handy.

looks.comment: The best look here. It finally solves d26 with forest green d12 and olive d41 in one earthy tonal family, and the navy d62 keeps cool colour at his face, all fully rideable on d55. A pale blue d02 collar under the merino would add the precision his DNA asks for.

failures.detail: Charcoal d05, grey d21, navy d30 and black d51 are exactly the navy-and-grey rut he wants to get out of, with no warmth or texture move to answer the aspiration.

'Sleeves left at full length suits his long arms' is not a technique; full length is the default. The claim that the blazer stays 'uncrushed' under a shell with a d60 backpack strapped over it is overstated.

The d42 technical shell over tailoring is functional but off-DNA. The d41 waxed jacket over the unstructured d30 is the Margaret Howell answer and just as rideable. Flannel d21 thighs will get wet below either hip-length jacket.

looks.comment: It is a sound, rideable adaptation of his proven presentation look and correctly avoids d40 and the tie. But it is the safe navy-grey-black answer. Swapping d21 for d26, or d42 for d41, would have made it his sharpest version rather than his usual one.

failures.detail: An open-collared d09 shirt puts rust collar and shoulders right at his jaw. The ecru d03 neckline only covers the throat, and the d62 scarf comes off indoors, so the claim that the rust 'stays further down' is false.
Brown suede d50 derbies on a showery, windy day are hedged rather than solved. Put d55 in the look from the start.
The rationale misdescribes where the colour sits, which teaches the client the wrong lesson about handling rust near his face.

looks.comment: Rust, ecru and navy is a good palette, and reviving d09 is the right instinct. As styled, though, the rust sits at the face he says it does not suit. It would work better with d09 worn closed under the d04 navy crew so only a sliver of collar shows, or with the rust kept below the face as an overshirt only once the face colour is handled. The d43 under d42 outer layering is also a technical full look on top.

judgement.missedOpportunity: A jacket-ready warm-texture look that answers both the aspiration and a possible client drop-in: d02 pale blue poplin under d12 forest green merino, with d26 chocolate cords, d30 navy unstructured blazer, d55 lug boots, d65 belt, d41 olive waxed jacket over the top for the ride, d62 scarf and d63 beanie.
judgement.summary: A thoughtful set with genuine range. It reaches for the neglected d26, d09 and d12, respects the cycling directive throughout, and sensibly excludes d36, d40 and d53. Look 1 is excellent and should lead. Look 2 is correct but stays in his navy-grey comfort zone and over-relies on a technical shell over tailoring. Look 3 has the right idea, but its explanation misstates where the rust sits relative to his face. Details are slightly loose throughout: a hidden belt, no beanie in wind, and suede hedged for rain.

results.requestText: Dinner with friends at a nice restaurant on Saturday night.

looks.title: Earth and Evergreen
looks.idea: Forest green and chocolate cord: the warm, textured dinner look he never wears, kept quiet.
looks.howToWear: Wear the forest green merino with the sleeves pushed to the forearm, since his long arms make a full-length sleeve look short when pulled down. Leave it untucked at the front only, with a half-tuck at the hip so the brown belt just shows. Let the cord trousers sit with a slight break over the lug-sole boots. Wear the waxed jacket and navy scarf for the ride, then take them off at the restaurant so the green and brown can show.
looks.why: The chocolate cord has only been worn twice, and this is the pairing that makes sense of it. Green and brown sit well with his cool colouring and give him the warmth and texture he says he lacks, with no mustard or orange near his face. The lug boots and waxed jacket handle wind and showers on the bike, and the look still reads as Margaret Howell rather than outdoor gear.

looks.title: Soft Tailoring, Roll-Neck
looks.idea: His proven presentation formula, loosened into an evening look with a soft blazer.
looks.howToWear: Wear the charcoal roll-neck tucked or half-tucked into the flannel trousers, with the black belt. Put the unstructured navy blazer over it with the sleeves just clear of the wrist. Leave the navy scarf loose, not tied. Ride in the rain shell over everything, then stow it in the backpack on arrival so the blazer is what people see.
looks.why: It repeats the charcoal roll-neck, grey flannel and Chelsea boots combination that felt sharp for him. The soft blazer adds a layer of tailoring without the stiffness of the suit that felt over the top. The rubber-soled Chelseas grip the pedals and handle wet pavements, and the blazer has enough shape for a nice restaurant.

looks.title: Cardigan and Pale Blue
looks.idea: A shawl cardigan over a cool blue shirt: relaxed warmth with a precise collar.
looks.howToWear: Wear the pale blue poplin shirt with the top button open and the collar flat over the shawl collar of the oatmeal cardigan. Leave the cardigan open or fastened with one button. Roll the shirt cuffs once under the cardigan sleeve. Tuck the shirt into the navy pleated trousers and wear the brown belt. Wear the waxed jacket on the ride and hang it up at the restaurant.
looks.why: The oatmeal chunky knit brings texture and warmth to navy trousers he already trusts. Pale blue is flattering against his grey-blue eyes. The proportions are relaxed but clean, and none of the pieces is formal enough to look stiff.

output.note: I've assumed you're cycling to dinner, so no look uses the overcoat, the loafers or the Oxfords (slippery on wet pedals). If you're getting a taxi, swap the navy overcoat in for the outerwear in look 2 or 3. I've left the camel suede trucker out because of the showers, and the wardrobe has no waterproof smart layer for it. A mid-weight dark jacket that works on the bike and at dinner would fill that gap.

failures.detail: For a 'nice restaurant' the look stops at a fine merino crew (d12) over wide-wale cord (d26). Once the waxed jacket (d41) comes off, nothing tailored remains. The navy unstructured blazer (d30) over d12 would lift it to the right register and keep his tailored DNA.

'Untucked at the front only, with a half-tuck at the hip' contradicts itself and can't be followed. A fussy half-tuck on a fine merino crew also reads as tried-hard, which is the opposite of what he wants. Wear it straight over the belt or fully tucked.

It claims green and brown 'sit well with his cool colouring'. Chocolate is a warm brown; it works here because it is on the legs and the cool forest green is at the face. Saying that would have taught him something.

looks.comment: This is the right instinct: it finally gives the rarely-worn d26 a job, and green with chocolate delivers the warmth and texture he asked for. As sent, though, it is a Saturday-afternoon look rather than a nice dinner. Add d30 and fix the tuck instruction and it becomes the best look of the three.
